name: Gareth Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What happens on your factory shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate a plastic injection-moulding press that makes small valve housings. I set the mould, watch the temperature and check the first pieces for sink marks before they go to packing. I have worked this press for years, hold a vocational certificate and do an ordinary, sound job. The pay is lower than many operators get, and I cannot claim to be the plant expert.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your household situation and how do you use new technology?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Alia drives a community transport van, and our grown son has moved out. We rent and have about three weeks of expenses saved. There are only a few comparable plants within reach. I use an AI tool now and then to explain a moulding term, but I check the machine book and ask the setter before changing heat. I will take up a new tool once somebody else has made it work on this press. I am 58 and would like to retire eventually, although we do not know if our income could cover rent then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the moulding crew that faster order plans do not change the first-piece check. A sink mark on a valve housing will still reach a customer if we rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two wages pay the rent now, but three weeks saved leaves almost no room for a missed pay period. I know this press and would like steady hours while I work out retirement costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep checking the first moulded housings after a changeover and ask the setter about an odd temperature. If an extra paid shift appears, I would add some of that new wage to our emergency savings after rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about money even when the work itself stays familiar. The quiet picture is easier to face because the pay keeps coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is a sink mark to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A shallow dent where the plastic cools unevenly. I tilt the first valve housing under a lamp before the rest of the run is packed. You can miss the dent looking straight down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let an AI tool set temperature?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I use it to understand a term, not to turn the press dial. The approved machine book and the setter decide the range. I would need a supervised test before a new control became routine.

say: I would **keep** first-piece checks while order plans become faster.
A **rushed** run can send marked valve housings to customers.
think: **Current** wages pay rent, but three weeks saved leaves little margin.
I would **value** steady shifts while estimating retirement costs.
do: **Keep** inspecting first housings and asking the setter about heat.
**Add** new extra-shift wages to emergency savings after rent and food.
feel: **Uneasy** about thin reserves despite continued familiar work.
S0.quote: I tilt the first valve housing under a lamp before the rest of the run is packed.
fieldNote: **Gareth** is an experienced average-skill injection-moulding operator with a vocational certificate and lower pay.

steps.text: Keep checking first valve housings after mould changes
Save newly paid extra-shift wages after rent and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor which office plans change first and whether a robot is actually due to unload our press. I want the setter to see a full guarded run before anyone loses hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot unloader could leave fewer people on the moulding shift later. I am experienced but not the specialist they would retain first. Three weeks saved would not buy much job-search time, and local openings are scarce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to watch a guarded unloading trial and compare damaged housings with our usual reject count. If the plant offers paid instruction on a new AI fault display, I would learn that screen with the setter and check its warning against the machine book. I would apply for a posted local quality-checking job only if the net pay after travel and shifts cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about hours. I could learn a proven screen, but I would not run a robot from one demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would let you operate the unloader?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An offered funded paid place with a fitter teaching safe stops and lockout, followed by supervised practice on a real press. I would accept that if the class fits my shift. Watching it unload a tray is not enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no checking vacancy is posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the present wage and look at actual nearby moulding jobs, few as they are. I would compare pay after travel and shifts before applying. Alia’s driving wage cannot carry all the rent alone.

say: I would **ask** for a guarded robot run and written staffing terms.
**Office** planning changes precede physical press unloading.
think: A **robot** may cut moulding shifts even for experienced operators.
**Three** weeks saved and few local jobs mean little search time.
do: **Request** guarded unloading trial and compare damaged housings.
**Learn** offered AI fault screen on paid time with setter and book checks.
**Apply** for posted quality work only with rent-covering net pay after travel and shifts.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, open to proven tools with supervised practice.
S1.quote: I could learn a proven screen, but I would not run a robot from one demonstration.
fieldNote: **Gareth** would learn a new AI fault display only with offered paid instruction and machine-book checks.
He **observes** a robot trial; operating the unloader requires a separate offered funded paid supervised place.
**Quality** and fallback jobs each need real postings, enough net pay after travel and workable shifts.

steps.text: Request guarded unloading trial and compare reject counts
Learn offered AI fault display on paid time with setter checks
Apply for posted quality job only with rent-covering net pay after travel and shifts
Check posted moulding work if no quality vacancy and pay after travel and shifts fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the line AGI may change orders in 2028, while capable robots loading, clearing and checking our press around 2031 are the larger risk to hours. We need a written staffing plan before that second date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most operator shifts to go if robots can handle a whole moulding run. I will be 63 then. Three weeks saved would vanish, and Alia’s wage alone might not meet rent; I would lie awake wondering how to cover the next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would cancel the planned trip to see our son and write out rent, power and food. I would ask the landlord about payment timing before any missed rent and ask the factory for written redeployment terms. I would apply for a posted local inspection job only if it includes paid supervised safety training and net pay after travel and hours that cover the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed by the expected shift loss. I can keep a level voice at work and still be frightened about the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the moulding certificate move you to maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It teaches this press, not robot lockout. I would need a funded paid practical course with a fitter before entering a robot cell. I would not present my certificate as a licence I do not have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your son for rent money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He has his own home costs. I might ask him to help compare job adverts, but I would not assume he could pay our rent. We need written work or lender terms, not a family guess.

say: I would **separate** 2028 order AGI from hands-on moulding robots around 2031.
I would **demand** written staffing terms before robot installation.
think: **Three** weeks saved and one remaining wage may not pay rent.
do: **Cancel** family trip and list essential bills.
**Ask** landlord about timing and factory for redeployment terms.
**Apply** for posted inspection work only with paid safety training and bill-covering net wage and shifts.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless rent worry.
S2.quote: I can keep a level voice at work and still be frightened about the rent.
fieldNote: **Gareth** expects physical robot work to displace moulding shifts around 2031, about three years after AGI changes orders.
His **experience** does not offset a three-week reserve and few nearby openings if the lower wage disappears.
**Any** inspection application requires an actual posting, paid supervised safety training and net pay after travel covering bills.

steps.text: Cancel planned family trip and list rent power and food bills
Ask landlord about payment timing before missed rent
Ask factory for written redeployment terms
Apply for posted inspection work with paid safety training bill-covering net pay after travel and shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the supervisor that five years is enough to teach operators safe robot work, if the plant pays for a real course. AGI changes orders in 2031 and capable robots tend the press around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 66 by that robot date. I know this mould well, but I have never proved a robot arm is isolated. Retirement may be close in age; we cannot assume it pays the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enrol in an offered recognised moulding-inspection course only if it is funded, keeps my class hours paid and includes supervised robot stop and lockout practice on a workable shift. After qualifying, I would apply for a posted local inspection role only if net pay after travel and its hours cover our rent. If no paid place opens, I would stay on the press and search posted local moulding jobs with sufficient wages and shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing wages while trying to learn. A good robot-safety course has to be a real paid place, not a leaflet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would an online AI lesson help first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might explain a term, but it cannot show that the robot arm is dead. I need the fitter to watch me stop and test the cell. I would only take responsibility after supervised practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you stop full shifts at 66?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alia and I would need written retirement-income estimates alongside our rent and living costs. We have not done that calculation. If it falls short, I need work and an actual posted opening.

say: I would **ask** for a recognised paid practical course before 2034.
2031 **order** changes come before capable hands-on press robots.
think: At 66, **moulding** experience does not establish robot safety skill.
**Retirement** income might not pay our rent and ordinary household bills.
do: **Enrol** in offered recognised funded paid course with supervised lockout and workable shift.
**Apply** after qualifying for posted inspection job only with rent-covering net pay after travel and hours.
If **no** paid course, seek posted moulding jobs with sufficient wages and shifts.
feel: **Anxious** about wages during learning and a real later vacancy.
S3.quote: A good robot-safety course has to be a real paid place, not a leaflet.
fieldNote: **Gareth** would enrol only in an offered recognised funded paid course with supervised stops and lockout on a workable shift.
**After** training he would separately apply for a posted job if net pay after travel and hours cover rent.
**Without** a paid place he keeps his wage and checks posted local moulding jobs.

steps.text: Enrol in offered funded paid recognised course with supervised lockout and workable shift
Apply after qualification for posted inspection work only with rent-covering net pay after travel and hours
Seek posted moulding work if no course and wages and shifts suffice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our son that ten years gives us time to count retirement costs and ask the plant for a safe paid route if I still need a wage. AGI changes orders in 2036, and capable robots reach the moulding press around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 68 at the first date and 71 by the robot date. Alia and I hope to have stopped full shifts, but our current three-week reserve is no proof we can. If income figures fall short, paid work remains necessary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request written estimates of retirement income and household costs. If we still need wages, I would take an offered recognised funded course on paid workable hours with supervised robot lockout, then apply for a posted local inspection role only if net pay after travel and shifts cover rent. If no paid course is offered, I would check posted moulding work with viable wages and hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about how far away the numbers are. A longer warning only helps if we turn it into real figures and real course terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your son to know about this job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show him a rejected valve housing and explain why cooling leaves a sink mark. A small dent tells you the moulding process needs attention. That knowledge is worth passing on while I have the shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use savings to retire at 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three weeks saved is a repair fund, not retirement income. I would compare written monthly income with rent and food before choosing any exit date. If the figures do not cover us, I will look for paid work.

say: I would **request** real retirement figures and safe paid course terms.
2036 **order** AI precedes hands-on moulding robots around 2039.
think: At 68 in 2036 I **may** have left shifts if income covers rent.
At 71 **near** 2039 employment depends on actual figures.
do: **Request** written retirement income and cost estimates.
If **still** working, take offered funded paid safe course on workable hours.
**After** qualification, apply for posted inspection work only with rent-covering net pay and shifts.
feel: **Uneasy** about uncertain income, willing to plan with written terms.
S4.quote: Three weeks saved is a repair fund, not retirement income.
fieldNote: **Gareth** assumes neither a pension nor continued factory employment at 71; written figures determine the outcome.
If **wages** remain necessary, retraining requires an offered recognised funded paid place with supervised safety.
A **posted** inspection job needs enough net pay after travel; without a course he checks viable posted moulding work.

steps.text: Request written retirement income and household cost figures
Take offered funded paid recognised course if work needed with supervised lockout and shifts
Apply after course for posted inspection work only with rent-covering net pay after travel and shifts

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most because capable robots could remove my moulding shifts around 2031 while we have only three weeks saved. A paid practical safety course and a posted local job with enough net pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I have worked the moulding press long enough to know what a tiny dent means. A small dent tells you the moulding process needs attention.
